st.headline: He gave up an iron rice bowl and sold his home to chase his business dreams
st.teaser: Kelvin Hong has had a passion for economics since his university days.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Kelvin Hong spent seven years in the civil service before giving up the security of public service to pursue his entrepreneurial dream – establishing a vocational school and a chain of spa and wellness outlets.
As a civil servant, he worked on economic policy, including writing the first policy paper setting out the Government’s approach to fighting SARS, or s evere acute respiratory syndrome.
Having previously enjoyed the security of an “iron rice bowl” career, he now had to make difficult financial decisions to fund his business.

He sold his condominium unit and moved his family of five to a rental property, and later downsized to an HDB resale flat, all while dealing with the uncertainty of running a business and providing for his family.
He sold his chain of wellness outlets in 2010.

“Education has always been a passion of mine. I’ve been tutoring since my university days and have accumulated about 28 years of experience teaching economics,” said Hong, 52, who founded The Economics Tutor in 1998 while running other businesses.
Throughout his entrepreneurial journey, he continued to tutor in economics, a passion he had developed at university.
After selling his other businesses, he decided to focus fully on tuition.
Today, Hong is the founder and principal tutor of The Economics Tutor and Ace GP Tuition, where he helps pre-university students build a strong foundation in economics and General Paper.
He graduated from the National University of Singapore with a Bachelor of Social Sciences, with first-class honours in economics.
His wife, 50, is also his partner in the tuition business, and they have three children aged 22, 20 and 11.
The Economics Tutor and Ace GP Tuition are my current ventures. I have run and sold off other businesses over the last two decades.

I prefer investing in my businesses because making money on its own has never given me much joy. What I enjoy is creating something and developing it until it succeeds, because by then, it adds real value to society. I am also considering other business ventures in the tech and education space.

I don’t own any individual stocks at the moment. My savings sit in safe assets. They won’t make anyone rich, but they’re secure. I’ve been tempted to buy a few individual stocks over the past year, but prices have looked too high to me, so I’m keeping dry powder and waiting for a correction rather than chasing the market. Knowing when not to invest is part of investing too.

My children’s education isn’t a financial asset in the usual sense, but it’s the investment I’m most certain of. Besides carefully choosing tuition that deepens their understanding and mastery beyond exams, I invest heavily in building their competencies: carpentry, baking, art and craft, music, robotics, various sports and communication skills, as well as their own little start- ups.
On paper, probably my home. But the asset that actually pays the bills is my tuition business. Unlike most assets, it doesn’t depreciate as long as I keep using it.
Spend less than you earn, don’t borrow what you can’t comfortably repay, don’t buy what you don’t understand, work really hard, and be patient.

None of it is original, but after working on economic policy and then running businesses through good years and bad, I’ve found that most financial disasters come from impatience: wanting the return without putting in the time or effort.

A lot of what passes for investment advice online today is really marketing. If someone is promising high returns with no risk, the question I’d ask is – who is actually making money from the arrangement?

No. As an economist, I find it hard to love an asset that pays no income and whose value depends entirely on another person fancying it. The closest I came to tangible assets was a small property portfolio, which I have since sold.

My first real investment, in the sense of putting serious money at risk, was buying some stocks on the Singapore Exchange and some unit trusts. I don’t think they fared well. I was a greenhorn who had just started earning serious money and was happily experimenting. In hindsight, there are cheaper ways to learn.

In a previous business, an overseas outlet ended in a six-figure loss. Looking back, I had made the classic mistake of planning around the demand I hoped for rather than the demand I could actually see. I now use that outlet as a case study when I teach company strategies. Students remember a real six-figure mistake far better than a textbook example.

My best financial decision was to sell off, in 2010, my chain of wellness outlets. It was a multimillion-dollar business, but my greatest returns came in the form of a sabbatical to reset my spiritual condition, including my lifestyle and life goals.

I traded in my business world back then for my soul, and it has been my best investment to date. During those sabbatical years, I was still providing tuition, albeit on a very small scale, and I have built it up since then into my current ventures.
My mum was a homemaker and my dad was a senior executive in a multinational corporation. It was a comfortable childhood, and maybe that is why I was rather spendthrift as a young adult.

I did start working early, selling Newsweek subscription s and tutoring during my varsity days, so I was earning my own money from about 18. That taught me what an hour of my time was worth, and that the most reliable way to earn more was to become better at something people needed.
Selling Newsweek subscriptions in schools during the holidays was my first lesson in selling – a few minutes in front of strangers to make my case and far more noes than yeses.

I learnt that selling is mostly about informing people in a persuasive way, which turns out not to be so different from teaching. I don’t remember exactly what it paid, but it was decent money for someone my age.
I don’t recall actually saving up for anything. I was more of a spender as a child. I learnt to save only as I became wiser and more mature.
My students sometimes assume I live a lavish, branded lifestyle, and I tell them it’s quite the opposite: When I need to shop, I mostly do it online or in Johor Bahru.

cna.headline: Verstappen wins in Las Vegas for third time in four years
cna.teaser: Verstappen wins in Las Vegas for third time in four years
fullText: LAS VEGAS, Nov 21 : Red Bull's Max Verstappen won a crazy, slipstreaming Las Vegas Grand Prix for the third time in four years on Saturday, while Mercedes rival George Russell hit the barriers late on and finished ninth.

In a race of 35 lead changes over 50 laps, and drivers nose-to-tail under the floodlights with track advantage swinging back and forth like a yo-yo, McLaren's 2025 champion Lando Norris and teammate Oscar Piastri finished second and third behind the polesitter.
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collided again in a race in which both collected 10-second penalties for separate incidents and finished seventh and 10th respectively.
"That was crazy. Really, really surreal and something I've never seen before in Formula One myself," said Verstappen, who beat Norris by 0.639 seconds.

Mercedes have already won both titles, with 20-year-old Italian Kimi Antonelli this month becoming the youngest ever Formula One world champion, while Verstappen and Russell started the weekend scrapping to end the season as overall runner-up.
Verstappen's fourth win in six races sent him 37 points clear of Ferrari's Hamilton with Russell, who started on the front row, dropping to fourth overall and level with Norris.
Antonelli was fourth with Alpine's Pierre Gasly fifth and teammate Franco Colapinto sixth. Carlos Sainz was eighth for Williams in the Spaniard's 250th race.
"I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula One," said Norris.
"I didn't know what was happening half the time. I didn't know if I was going to have the best race and have a chance to win or end up last. It had everything this race."
Piastri, who started 17th, could only agree.
"They say Las Vegas is the entertainment capital of the world and that was pretty entertaining to be a part of," said the Australian.
"It was pretty random. You would pass someone on one straight super easy, then the next straight you would struggle and then with someone else it would be different strengths and weaknesses."
(Writing by Alan Baldwin in London, editing by Peter Rutherford)
A single handpicked story that we think you shouldn't miss. Just one a day.

listening.title: Singapore Expands Electric Bus Fleet to Cut Urban Emissions
listening.transcript: Singapore's Land Transport Authority has announced plans to deploy hundreds of new electric buses across public routes by next year. Officials stated that replacing traditional diesel vehicles will significantly reduce urban carbon emissions and noise pollution. commuters can look forward to quieter journeys and improved air quality along major trunk routes. The initiative forms part of the nation's broader Green Plan 2030.

economistArticle.title: The Lonely Yields: Why China is Bucking Global Bond Trends
paras: Across major developed economies, sovereign bond yields have drifted steadily upward as central banks grapple with sticky inflation and elevated policy rates. From Washington to Frankfurt, institutional investors are demanding higher returns to lock up their capital in government debt. Yet in Beijing, a starkly different economic narrative is unfolding. Yields on Chinese sovereign bonds have plummeted to historic lows as the country struggles with persistent domestic demand weakness and lingering real estate troubles.

To counter this economic inertia, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) has taken the opposite path of its Western peers by repeatedly cutting benchmark interest rates. In theory, cheaper borrowing costs ought to spur commercial investment and reignite consumer spending. In practice, however, risk-averse commercial banks and anxious household savers have poured massive sums into government bonds, driving prices up and yields down to levels that trouble senior policymakers.

The central bank finds itself in an awkward predicament. While it desires low interest rates to invigorate domestic growth, it worries that excessively low long-term bond yields signal deep institutional pessimism about China's future growth trajectory. Furthermore, ultra-low Chinese yields put downward pressure on the renminbi, encouraging capital flight to higher-yielding offshore dollar assets and threatening currency stability.

In response, Chinese authorities have attempted an unusual regulatory intervention by issuing stern warnings to domestic financial institutions against over-investing in long-term sovereign debt. Policymakers have even signaled a willingness to sell bonds from their own balance sheet to artificially push yields back up. Yet such verbal and market interventions highlight a fundamental tension between stimulating a sluggish real economy and curbing market speculation.

Until consumer confidence returns and the embattled property sector stabilizes, investors will likely continue seeking safety in government debt. China's central bank may keep trimming rates to aid economic recovery, but forcing sovereign bond yields higher in a lukewarm economy remains a delicate, if not contradictory, balancing act.
economistArticle.cn:
全球主要发达经济体的国债收益率随央行应对粘性通胀和高政策利率而稳步攀升。从华盛顿到法兰克福，机构投资者正要求更高的回报率以锁定政府债券资金。然而在北京，一个截然不同的经济故事正在上演。由于国内需求持续疲软以及房地产业危机未消，中国国债收益率已暴跌至历史低点。

为了应对这种经济惯性下滑，中国人民银行采取了与西方同行相反的路径，屡次下调基准利率。理论上，较低的融资成本应当能刺激企业投资并重新点燃消费支出。然而在实践中，避险心切的商业银行和焦虑的家庭储户将巨额资金涌入国债，从而拉高了债券价格，并将收益率推低至让决策层担忧的水平。

央行陷入了尴尬的困境。尽管它希望获得低利率来激活国内增长，但它担心极低的长期国债收益率反映出市场对中国未来增长轨迹的深层悲观情绪。此外，超低的中国收益率对人民币构成下行压力，促使资金流向海外的高收益美元资产，威胁货币稳定。

作为回应，中国监管层尝试进行罕见的监管干预，向国内金融机构发出严厉警告，要求其不要过度投资长期国债。决策者甚至表明愿意从自己的资产负债表中抛售国债，以人为推高收益率。然而，此类口头干预与市场干预凸显了刺激疲软的实业经济与遏制市场炒作之间的根本张力。

在消费者信心恢复且困境重重的房地产业稳定之前，投资者可能仍将继续在国债中寻求庇护。中国央行可能会继续降息以推行经济复苏，但在温吞的经济环境中强行推高国债收益率仍是一项微妙甚至自相矛盾的平衡术。
